techniques.name: Ridge Regression Surrogates
techniques.description: A ridge regression surrogate approximates a complex model with a linear equation fitted to the complex model's own predictions. The complex model is run on a set of inputs, and ridge regression, a linear model with a penalty that keeps coefficients stable when features are correlated, is fitted to reproduce its outputs. Each coefficient then shows roughly how far a feature moves the complex model's output, averaged over those inputs. Fidelity, often reported as R-squared (the share of the model's variation the surrogate reproduces on held-out inputs), shows how far the coefficients can be trusted. They describe the complex model, not the real world.

example_use_cases.description: A model-risk team at a bank fits a ridge surrogate to a gradient-boosted credit-scoring model's scores on a held-out sample, reports how closely the surrogate reproduces them, and uses the standardised coefficients to brief the model-risk committee on which inputs drive scores overall.

A hospital analytics team fits a ridge surrogate to a neural network that predicts readmission risk from tabular records, to check that the features driving the network's predictions overall, such as age and prior admissions, are plausible to clinicians. The findings concern the network, not what causes readmission.

An energy company's forecasting team fits a ridge surrogate to a neural-network load forecaster using a year of hourly weather and calendar inputs, and reads the standardised coefficients to confirm that temperature and time of day dominate. A low R-squared during heatwaves leads the team to record that the surrogate does not describe the model in that regime.

An insurer's compliance team gives a regulator a ridge surrogate of its pricing model together with held-out R-squared and a table of each feature's contribution to a sample of quotes, so the regulator can check the stated drivers against the model's actual outputs.

limitations.description: A linear surrogate cannot represent interactions or thresholds. Where the complex model relies on them, the surrogate fits its predictions poorly and its coefficients describe a different model. Report held-out R-squared and treat a low value as a failed surrogate.

A good average fit can hide poor fit in parts of the input space, such as rare groups or extreme values, so the coefficients may be wrong for exactly the cases that matter. Check fidelity within subgroups and near decision boundaries.
There is no agreed fidelity level above which a surrogate can be trusted. Whether 50%, 80% or 99% of variance explained is enough depends on the use, so the reviewer has to set and justify a cut-off.

Ridge shrinks every coefficient and shares weight between correlated features. Coefficient sizes depend on the penalty strength and on feature scaling, so compare them only after standardising the features, and report the penalty used.

The surrogate explains the complex model's behaviour on the sampled inputs, not the real-world link between features and outcomes. Reading its coefficients as causes, or as evidence about the data, will mislead.

resources.title: Extracting Tree-Structured Representations of Trained Networks
resources.abstract: A  significant  limitation  of  neural  networks  is  that  the  represen(cid:173) tations  they  learn  are  usually  incomprehensible  to  humans.  We  present a  novel algorithm , TREPAN,  for extracting comprehensible,  symbolic representations from  trained neural  networks.  Our algo(cid:173) rithm uses  queries to induce a  decision tree that approximates the  concept  represented by  a  given  network.  Our experiments demon(cid:173) strate that TREPAN is  able to produce decision trees that maintain  a high level of fidelity to their respective networks while being com(cid:173) prehensible  and  accurate.  Unlike  previous  work  in  this  area,  our  algorithm is  general in its applicability and scales well  to large net(cid:173) works  and problems with  high-dimensional input spaces.

resources.title: Interpretable Machine Learning: A Guide for Making Black Box Models Explainable

sample_claims.text: A ridge surrogate reproduces the credit model's scores on held-out applications with an R-squared of at least 0.9, and its five largest standardised coefficients identify the inputs that drive scores overall.
The surrogate of the readmission-risk model reproduces the model's predictions closely within every age band tested, so its coefficients describe the model's behaviour for each of those bands.

The demand-forecasting model depends mainly on temperature and time of day overall, as shown by a linear surrogate whose fit to the model has been measured, with the lower fit during heatwaves reported as a limit.
Where the linear surrogate's fit to the model falls below the stated threshold, the model is recorded as not summarised by a linear surrogate, and no coefficient is cited as an explanation of it.

The regulator holds the pricing model's ridge surrogate with its held-out R-squared and a table of each feature's contribution to a sample of quotes, and can check the stated drivers against the model's outputs.

techniques.name: RuleFit
techniques.description: RuleFit builds a predictive model that a person can read: a short list of if-then rules plus a few ordinary feature weights. It first trains an ensemble of decision trees (many small trees whose outputs are combined) and turns each branch into a candidate rule, such as 'IF age > 50 AND income < £30k'. It then fits a linear model over those rules and the original features using the lasso, a penalty that sets many weights to exactly zero, so only the most useful terms remain. The surviving rules and weights can be read directly, and each term has an importance score, overall and for single predictions. Fitted to real outcomes, the result can replace an opaque model; fitted to an opaque model's predictions, it is a surrogate that approximates that model, and its fit should then be checked.

example_use_cases.description: A telecoms analytics team fits RuleFit to the predictions of its gradient-boosted churn model rather than to the churn labels, to get a short list of rules that approximates the model. Marketing staff read the top rules, and the team reports how closely the rules reproduce the model's predictions before anyone relies on them.

A lender replaces an opaque default-risk model with a RuleFit model fitted to repayment outcomes. For one declined application, the importance scores show which few rules and income or debt terms drove its score, and the validation team checks them against credit policy.

A hospital team builds an admission-risk model as a RuleFit model fitted directly to patient outcomes, so that clinicians and the ethics committee can read the whole model, a few rules such as 'IF systolic_bp > 140 AND diabetes = true' plus a handful of weights. The team counts the active rules first and keeps the model only if it is short enough to read.

limitations.description: The lasso can leave many rules active, and a model with hundreds of active terms is no longer readable. Rules also approximate smooth linear trends poorly and need many pieces to do so. Count the non-zero terms before calling the model interpretable.

Rules overlap and are often correlated, so a rule's weight cannot be read on its own. 'Temperature above 15' is also true wherever 'temperature above 10' is. With correlated inputs, rules can also suggest interactions that are not in the real relationship.

Tree size sets how long rules can be and which interactions can appear. Shallow trees give short, readable rules but miss high-order interactions, and deep trees capture them at the cost of long rules. No single depth suits every problem.

Fitted to a black-box model's predictions, RuleFit only approximates that model. Without a fidelity check, such as agreement on held-out inputs, its rules describe the surrogate and may not describe the model they are meant to explain.

resources.title: Predictive learning via rule ensembles
resources.abstract: General regression and classification models are constructed as linear combinations of simple rules derived from the data. Each rule consists of a conjunction of a small number of simple statements concerning the values of individual input variables. These rule ensembles are shown to produce predictive accuracy comparable to the best methods. However, their principal advantage lies in interpretation. Because of its simple form, each rule is easy to understand, as is its influence on individual predictions, selected subsets of predictions, or globally over the entire space of joint input variable values. Similarly, the degree of relevance of the respective input variables can be assessed globally, locally in different regions of the input space, or at individual prediction points. Techniques are presented for automatically identifying those variables that are involved in interactions with other variables, the strength and degree of those interactions, as well as the identities of the other variables with which they interact. Graphical representations are used to visualize both main and interaction effects.

resources.title: RuleFit-Based Nomogram Using Inflammatory Indicators for Predicting Survival in Nasopharyngeal Carcinoma, a Bi-Center Study
resources.abstract: Purpose: Traditional prognostic studies utilized different cut-off values, without evaluating potential information contained in inflammation-related hematological indicators. Using the interpretable machine-learning algorithm RuleFit, this study aimed to explore valuable inflammatory rules reflecting prognosis in nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC) patients. Patients and Methods: In total, 1706 biopsy-proven NPC patients treated in two independent hospitals (1320 and 386) between January 2010 and March 2014 were included. RuleFit was used to develop risk-predictive rules using hematological indicators with no distributive difference between the two centers. Time-event-dependent hematological rules were further selected by stepwise multivariate Cox analysis. Combining high-efficiency hematological rules and clinical predictors, a final model was established. Models based on other algorithms (AutoML, Lasso) and clinical predictors were built for comparison, as well as a reported nomogram. Area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) and concordance index (C-index) were used to verify the predictive precision of different models. A site-based app was established for convenience. Results: RuleFit identified 22 combined baseline hematological rules, achieving AUROCs of 0.69 and 0.64 in the training and validation cohorts, respectively. By contrast, the AUROCs of the optimal contrast model based on AutoML were 1.00 and 0.58. For overall survival, the final model had a much higher C-index than the base model using TN staging in two cohorts (0.769 vs 0.717, P < 0.001; 0.752 vs 0.688, P < 0.001), and showing great generalizability in training and validation cohorts. The two models based on RuleFit rules performed best, compared with other models. As for other endpoints, the final model showed a similar trend. Kaplan–Meier curve exhibited 22.9% (390/1706) patients were “misclassified” by AJCC staging, but the final model could assess risk classification accurately. Conclusion: The proposed final models based on inflammation-related rules based on RuleFit showed significantly elevated predictive performance.

sample_claims.text: The credit risk model's decision logic is expressible as a sparse set of interpretable if-then rules combined with linear feature weights
The patient risk score can be reconstructed from its intercept, active clinical-input rules and linear terms using the recorded clipping and weights.
The fraud detection model identifies risk through comprehensible rules that stakeholders can validate against domain knowledge
The churn-score approximation exposes its weighted rules and linear terms, with agreement assessed against the original model on the stated dataset.

techniques.name: Generalized Additive Models
techniques.description: A generalised additive model (GAM) builds its prediction by adding a baseline and one smooth curve for each input feature. It extends linear and logistic regression by letting each feature's effect bend, so the model can follow patterns such as risk that climbs steeply after a certain age. Each curve is learned from the data with a smoothing method, such as splines (flexible curves built from joined polynomial pieces). Plotting the curves shows how each feature moves the prediction across its range, so the model can be read directly without a separate explanation method. Because the curves are added together, the model does not capture the joint effect of two features unless a combined term is added by hand.

example_use_cases.description: A hospital builds its 30-day readmission model as a GAM so that its governance committee can audit it. The committee reviews one curve each for age, blood pressure and medication adherence, and queries any stretch where predicted risk falls as a known risk factor rises, since that can point to a data problem rather than a real effect.

A lender uses a GAM for credit scoring so that it can tell a declined applicant how income, credit history and debt-to-income ratio each moved their score. Each factor has its own curve, so the explanation comes straight from the model and needs no separate explanation tool.

An environmental agency models river nitrate levels with a GAM and plots the curve for rainfall. The curve shows the effect levelling off above a certain rainfall, which analysts report to catchment managers instead of a single regression coefficient.

limitations.description: Each feature acts separately, so the model cannot represent effects that depend on two features together, such as the impact of a dose varying with age. Product terms can be added by hand, but each must be thought of in advance and adds a surface that is harder to read than a curve.

The smoothness of each curve is a modelling choice. Cross-validation or penalised fitting selects it automatically, but too little smoothing gives wiggly curves that look like real effects and too much hides genuine bends, so each curve should be read with its confidence band.

When features are strongly related, such as income and age, a nonlinear form of collinearity called concurvity lets one curve absorb part of another's effect. The individual curves can then misstate how much each feature influences the prediction.

A model with dozens of smooth terms produces dozens of curves. Reading them all is slow, so reviewers tend to inspect only the largest effects, and the transparency benefit shrinks as the number of terms grows.
Terms add on the chosen link scale. In a logistic GAM they are contributions to log-odds, not independent additions to readmission probability or guaranteed causal feature effects.

resources.title: mgcv: Mixed GAM Computation Vehicle with Automatic Smoothness Estimation
Generalized Additive Models
resources.abstract: Likelihood-based regression models such as the normal linear regression model and the linear logistic model, assume a linear (or some other parametric) form for the covariates X1, X2, …, Xp. We introduce the class of generalized additive models which replaces the linear form Σ βjXj by a sum of smooth functions Σ sj(Xj). The sj(·)'s are unspecified functions that are estimated using a scatterplot smoother, in an iterative procedure we call the local scoring algorithm. The technique is applicable to any likelihood-based regression model: the class of generalized linear models contains many of these. In this class the linear predictor η = Σ βjXj is replaced by the additive predictor Σ sj(Xj); hence, the name generalized additive models. We illustrate the technique with binary response and survival data. In both cases, the method proves to be useful in uncovering nonlinear covariate effects. It has the advantage of being completely automatic, i.e., no "detective work" is needed on the part of the statistician. As a theoretical underpinning, the technique is viewed as an empirical method of maximizing the expected log likelihood, or equivalently, of minimizing the Kullback-Leibler distance to the true model.

resources.title: Fast Stable Restricted Maximum Likelihood and Marginal Likelihood Estimation of Semiparametric Generalized Linear Models
resources.abstract: Recent work by Reiss and Ogden provides a theoretical basis for sometimes preferring restricted maximum likelihood (REML) to generalized cross-validation (GCV) for smoothing parameter selection in semiparametric regression. However, existing REML or marginal likelihood (ML) based methods for semiparametric generalized linear models (GLMs) use iterative REML or ML estimation of the smoothing parameters of working linear approximations to the GLM. Such indirect schemes need not converge and fail to do so in a non-negligible proportion of practical analyses. By contrast, very reliable prediction error criteria smoothing parameter selection methods are available, based on direct optimization of GCV, or related criteria, for the GLM itself. Since such methods directly optimize properly defined functions of the smoothing parameters, they have much more reliable convergence properties. The paper develops the first such method for REML or ML estimation of smoothing parameters. A Laplace approximation is used to obtain an approximate REML or ML for any GLM, which is suitable for efficient direct optimization. This REML or ML criterion requires that Newton–Raphson iteration, rather than Fisher scoring, be used for GLM fitting, and a computationally stable approach to this is proposed. The REML or ML criterion itself is optimized by a Newton method, with the derivatives required obtained by a mixture of implicit differentiation and direct methods. The method will cope with numerical rank deficiency in the fitted model and in fact provides a slight improvement in numerical robustness on the earlier method of Wood for prediction error criteria based smoothness selection. Simulation results suggest that the new REML and ML methods offer some improvement in mean-square error performance relative to GCV or Akaike’s information criterion in most cases, without the small number of severe undersmoothing failures to which Akaike’s information criterion and GCV are prone. This is achieved at the same computational cost as GCV or Akaike’s information criterion. The new approach also eliminates the convergence failures of previous REML- or ML-based approaches for penalized GLMs and usually has lower computational cost than these alternatives. Example applications are presented in adaptive smoothing, scalar on function regression and generalized additive model selection.

resources.title: A Tour of pyGAM — pyGAM documentation
Intelligible Models for HealthCare
resources.abstract: In machine learning often a tradeoff must be made between accuracy and intelligibility. More accurate models such as boosted trees, random forests, and neural nets usually are not intelligible, but more intelligible models such as logistic regression, naive-Bayes, and single decision trees often have significantly worse accuracy. This tradeoff sometimes limits the accuracy of models that can be applied in mission-critical applications such as healthcare where being able to understand, validate, edit, and trust a learned model is important. We present two case studies where high-performance generalized additive models with pairwise interactions (GA2Ms) are applied to real healthcare problems yielding intelligible models with state-of-the-art accuracy. In the pneumonia risk prediction case study, the intelligible model uncovers surprising patterns in the data that previously had prevented complex learned models from being fielded in this domain, but because it is intelligible and modular allows these patterns to be recognized and removed. In the 30-day hospital readmission case study, we show that the same methods scale to large datasets containing hundreds of thousands of patients and thousands of attributes while remaining intelligible and providing accuracy comparable to the best (unintelligible) machine learning methods.

sample_claims.text: Every input to the readmission risk model acts through a single plotted curve, so a clinician can read off how predicted risk changes with each input without running a separate explanation method.
The direction of each applicant attribute's effect in the credit model, as plotted with its confidence band, matches what credit risk specialists expect, and any departure has been explained.
The resource allocation model's score for any case is a baseline plus one contribution per policy factor, so each factor's share of a decision can be stated and audited.
Each nonlinear effect the model reports departs from a straight line by more than the width of its confidence band, so the bend is not an artefact of over-flexible smoothing.
